children: India has a “once in a generation” opportunity to move beyond semiconductor engineering and capture a larger share of the global value created through chip and system innovation, according to Vikram Meghal, SVP Engineering, Infosys.

Delivering a keynote at SEMICON India 2026 on Friday, Meghal said the semiconductor industry is shifting from a focus on packing more transistors into chips to system-level scaling, driven by the rapid growth of AI and specialised chips for different applications.
“Now it’s getting into more system-level scaling, which is the need of the hour, not just how many transistors you can pack in a certain area,” he said.

AI is emerging as a major driver of semiconductor demand, with AI data centre spending projected to rise by $6.7 trillion in the coming years, of which 50% is expected to go towards compute, memory and networking chips, Meghal said.

He said the changing demand environment, geopolitical pressures on semiconductor supply chains and the increasing use of AI in chip development were creating an opportunity for India to move up the value chain.
“This is allowing us to crunch the chip-to-fab time frame in a big way, and also allowing us to re-imagine the manufacturing process and re-engineer the entire life cycle,” he said.

Meghal identified three opportunities for India — “made for India”, “engineered in India” and “invent in India”. While India has already built significant engineering capabilities, he said the next phase should focus on developing products and intellectual property for global markets.

“In India, ER&D will potentially grow by 1.8 times in the next few years. The industry acknowledges that engineered in India is the best way to do it. Everybody is now discussing how to ‘invent in India’. So far, we have only been capturing the engineered-in-India value.

Now there is potential for global products to capture the innovation value and start looking at inventing in India. That’s where we will do justice to the decades of investment in building this ecosystem. The simple idea is: how to make India the innovation and engineering hub for the world,” he said.

According to Meghal, global customer development spending is expected to rise from $67 billion to $200 billion as specialised chips are developed for different applications. India has so far captured a significant part of the engineering value, but there is an opportunity to capture more of the innovation value.

The shift will require India to think beyond individual chips and build capabilities across the wider system, he said. India would need stronger capabilities in system-level performance, power and area optimisation, multi-die design, verification, regulatory compliance and product strategy.
“But the most important one is the product mindset. That is a combination of system thinking, ability to do product strategy, and ensuring we can drive product monetization,” he said.

Meghal cited Infosys’ work with a US semiconductor startup as an example of the value that could be captured. The company helped engineer a complex chip for fabric connectivity in a GPU on TSMC’s five-nanometre process. While the concept was developed in the US, the chip was completely engineered in India.

“The concept was developed in the US while the chip was engineered here. It was on a TSMC 5nm process, a complex chip. But the value we captured was probably in tens of millions, whereas the valuation for that concept was hundreds of millions,” he said.

title: India can move from ‘engineered in India’ to ‘invent in India’ in semiconductors: Infosys
